title: Vesak, the full moon
hookLine: many Buddhists mark the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing on the full moon of Vesakha

cards: Night in Colombo, in Sri Lanka. Streets hung with paper lanterns, some towering over the people below, lit from inside. Free food stalls handing out rice and tea to anyone passing, no money asked.
White-clad families walking to the temple with flowers and oil lamps. And overhead, a full moon. Across Asia and far beyond, many Buddhists keep this night as a high point of their year.
The Buddhist visit closes with it. Vesak, the full moon.

teach.b: Vesak takes its name from Vesakha, a month in the old Indian calendar, and the festival falls on its full moon, usually in April or May.

In the Theravada tradition, followed in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, Buddhists hold that three great events in the Buddha's life all happened on that same full moon: his birth in Lumbini, his awakening under the tree at Bodh Gaya, and his passing into final nirvana at Kushinagar.
One night for a whole life.
Other Buddhist traditions keep the calendar differently. In much of East Asia, the Buddha's birthday is its own festival, and in Japan his awakening is often marked separately, in December.
In Tibet, a whole holy month, Saga Dawa, marks these events. So once again, who you ask matters. For such a big night, what people do on Vesak is quiet.
They visit the temple, offer flowers, light lamps and incense. Many keep extra precepts for the day, eating simply and avoiding harm. And they give: food, lanterns, help.

On the Buddha's birthday in East Asia, people pour scented water over a small statue of the baby Buddha. In 1999 the United Nations recognized the Day of Vesak internationally. And that closes the week with Buddhists.
The man under the tree who woke up. Dukkha, and the way through. Anicca, this too.
Metta, may all beings be well. The middle way and Sona's lute. The three refuges.
And a full moon to hold them all.

how: On Vesak many Buddhists visit temples, offer flowers and lamps, keep extra precepts, listen to teachings and give food and help; in Sri Lanka streets fill with lanterns and free food stalls called dansal.

games.q: it's Vesak night in Colombo. you've set up a stall on your street. what do you do with the food?
o: give it away to anyone passing.
games.why: on Vesak many Sri Lankans run dansal, free food stalls, giving to anyone who passes. giving is one of the heart practices of the night.

practice: If the moon is up and you can see it, go and look; if not, picture a full moon rising over a temple roof, round and white. Let one thing from this week come back to you, and let the moon hold it.

wordCard.voice: Vesak. The full moon of Vesakha, when many Buddhists mark the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, with lamps, flowers and giving. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: Vesakha, the month whose full moon is Vesak.

carryVoice: Your line: the full moon. Lamps, flowers and food given freely, all under one moon. Day two hundred forty-five, and the Buddhist visit is complete.
